demo.name: Privilege demo (Cedar policy enforcement for MCP tool calls)

glossary.definition: A token whose act claim is an object with a sub, for example Dot acting for Mark. The server maps act.sub to context.token.actor and evaluates the call as the unattended action mcp:InvokeUnattended, so rules that limit an agent acting alone apply. A string-valued act is rejected, not guessed at.

An annotation on a forbid, for example @approvers("priya"). A denial by that policy becomes a hold for the named people, but only when every forbid that fired names approvers and the same call would be allowed with one approval.

The open-source policy language used for the AI Policies in this demo. A policy is a permit or a forbid over a principal, an action and a resource, with optional when and unless conditions on the request context.

The facts about one request that a Cedar condition can read: context.app (which MCP app), context.args.amount (the one tool argument Cedar sees), context.token.scopes, context.token.client_id, context.token.actor, context.approval_count, and the pinned and observed schema hashes. Free text such as an approval justification never reaches Cedar.
Cedar has no implicit allow: a request that no permit matches is denied. The decision then names the rule default-deny, because there is no deciding policy id to show.
A Cedar policy that refuses a request. A matching forbid beats every permit, so a hard limit such as the 10000 cap on book_fare stays a limit however many permits say yes.

The third outcome beside allow and deny. The call does not run and waits for a named approver; approving re-evaluates the call with approval_count 1 and runs the tool at most once. An unanswered hold expires after 10 minutes and counts as a deny.

The server code in front of the tools. Its enforce() function is the only path to a tool: it checks the arguments against the tool schema, asks Cedar for a decision, then runs the tool (allow), refuses (deny) or creates an approval (hold).
A Cedar policy that allows a request. A permit has no effect when any forbid also matches, and nothing is allowed unless some permit matches.
Who is asking. The verified sub claim becomes the principal User, and the groups claim becomes its parent Groups, so a policy can say principal in Group::"analysts". Cedar never sees the JWT itself.

Each tool is pinned by a hash of its name, description and schema when it is onboarded. A forbid denies any call when the hash the server advertises now no longer matches the pinned one, so approval is for a specific tool, not a name.

cards.label: A booking needs a second pair of eyes
cards.description: Dot books a fare over 1000 for Mark. The call is held, Priya approves, and it runs once.

cards.label: Mary gets two of three tools
cards.description: Analysts may use Search and Ticketing; nothing permits Payments, so it is denied by default.

cards.label: The tool list changed overnight
cards.description: A tool's description changes under the same name; the schema pin forbids the call.

cards.label: Cedar says no, even though another rule says yes
cards.description: A permit lets travel agents book fares; a hard cap of 10000 overrides it.

cards.label: Cedar policy language
cards.description: The language reference behind the demo's policies.

stories.title: A booking needs a second pair of eyes
stories.say: The agent did not get smarter permissions. A human stayed in the loop for exactly the risky one.

stories.title: Mary gets 2 of 3 tools
stories.say: The agent only gets what Mary is allowed to use, so it cannot be tricked into asking for more.

stories.title: The tool list changed overnight
stories.say: Approval is for a specific tool, not a name.

stories.title: Cedar says no, even though another rule says yes
stories.say: A hard limit stays a hard limit, however many rules say yes.
